name: Gruffudd Gryg
dates: fl. second half of the 14th century
credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gruffudd Gryg was an Anglesey bard of the second half of the fourteenth century, a contemporary of Dafydd ap Gwilym with whom he exchanged a famous poetic controversy that ended in an elegy each wrote for the other.
The poem here is a free English version after him, taken from George Borrow's Wild Wales and printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poems.title: The Yew Tree
poems.author: Gruffudd Gryg
poems.note: From "Wild Wales". Printed as "To the Yew Tree on the Grave of Dafydd ab Gwilym at Ystrad Flur. After Gruffydd Grug"; a free version, not a close translation.
poems.translator: trans. George Borrow (Welsh Poems and Ballads, 1915)
poems.text:
Thou noble tree; who shelt'rest kind
The dead man's house from winter's wind:
May lightnings never lay thee low,
Nor archer cut from thee his bow;
Nor Crispin peel thee pegs to frame,
But may thou ever bloom the same,
A noble tree the grave to guard
Of Cambria's most illustrious bard!
O tree of yew, which here I spy,
By Ystrad Flur's blest monast'ry,
Beneath thee lies, by cold Death bound,
The tongue for sweetness once renown'd.

Better for thee thy boughs to wave,
Though scath'd, above Ab Gwilym's grave,
Than stand in pristine glory drest
Where some ignobler bard doth rest;
I'd rather hear a taunting rhyme
From one who'll live through endless time,
Than hear my praises chanted loud
By poets of the vulgar crowd.
